properties.method: Computed by the Census Bureau from the 2020 TIGER geography. [verified]

blocks.text: Land area of [Ohio House District 4](../division/ohio-house-district-4-2020.yml) in the 2020 geography. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md), state legislative lower chamber file.

properties.mouth: 41.2875489, -84.3557802, in Defiance County. Joins the Maumee River. [inference]

blocks.text: The river that collects Allen County's drainage and carries it north to the Maumee at Defiance. [inference] It rises at 40.6669957, -83.8938286 and discharges at 41.2875489, -84.3557802 in Defiance County. [verified] — [USGS GNIS](../../catalog/gnis-domestic-names-ohio.md), feature 1065901. It gives its name to Auglaize Township in the county's south — one of the twelve townships recorded in the [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md). [verified]

Its significance to this corpus is directional. Allen County drains north to Lake Erie rather than south to the Ohio, and the Auglaize is the channel by which it does so. That single fact organizes a great deal: the county's swamp history, its canal, and the basin its water quality is accounted for in are all consequences of being on the Lake Erie side of the divide. [inference]

**It rises in this county**, at 40.6669957, -83.8938286 in Auglaize township — the township named after it. [verified] — [TIGERweb](../../catalog/tigerweb-census2020.md), point-in-polygon. So Allen County is not merely drained by the Auglaize; it is the ground the river starts on. See [where the Auglaize rises](../question/where-the-auglaize-rises.yml). Its whole subbasin, `04100007`, is one of the seven that make up the Maumee's drainage; the four blocks of that township on [the Scioto side](scioto-river-basin.yml) drain the opposite way, so the divide and this river's source are in the same township. [verified] — [USGS Watershed Boundary Dataset](../../catalog/usgs-watershed-boundary.md).

The glacially-formed wetland that covered much of northwest Ohio until it was drained in the second half of the nineteenth century. Allen County lies at its southern margin, and its northern townships were within it. [inference]

It belongs in this corpus because it is the negative space in the county's settlement history: the swamp is why this part of Ohio was settled late relative to the south of the state, why the drainage tile and ditch systems are as extensive as they are, and why the land is as productive as it is now that they exist. [inference] It is also a feature that no longer exists as such, which is a thing this class must be able to hold — a natural-feature node is not required to describe present ground.

**It has no GNIS record.** No feature named "Great Black Swamp" appears anywhere in the 17,921 rows of the Ohio file. [verified] — [USGS GNIS](../../catalog/gnis-domestic-names-ohio.md). That is not because the gazetteer omits vanished features: it carries 56 `Swamp` features in Ohio and marks the drained ones "(historical)" in the name itself. The likelier reason is that GNIS names features with a locatable point, and a wetland that covered much of northwest Ohio across a dozen counties does not have one. [inference] So this node keeps no identifier, and the absence is a fact about how gazetteers work rather than a gap in the retrieval.

nodes.label: Hog Creek

properties.mouth: 40.7708852, -83.9557761 — the head of the Ottawa River.

blocks.text: The stream that, joining Little Hog Creek, forms the Ottawa River. Its mouth is at 40.7708852, -83.9557761 and it rises at 40.7139417, -83.7221552 in the county's east. [verified] — [USGS GNIS](../../catalog/gnis-domestic-names-ohio.md), feature 1066038.

That mouth coordinate is the whole point of this node. It is identical, to seven decimal places, to the source coordinate GNIS gives for [the Ottawa River](ottawa-river.yml) and to the mouth GNIS gives for [Little Hog Creek](little-hog-creek.yml). Three records written by one authority place the same point at the end of two creeks and the head of a river, which is what a confluence looks like in a names file. [verified] — same source. Every `flows-into` edge in this corpus before this one was asserted from general knowledge.

Hog Creek is also the older name of the whole watercourse, and the corpus's [Ottawa River](ottawa-river.yml) node records the name surviving in local usage. GNIS is consistent with that and does not establish it: what the file shows is that the name attaches today to the upper tributary only. [inference]
Ohio has a second Hog Creek, in Champaign County — feature 1041646, and unrelated. [verified] — same source.

refusals: GNIS is consistent with that and does not establish it: what the file shows is that the name attaches today to the upper tributary only.

properties.mouth: 40.7708852, -83.9557761 — the head of the Ottawa River, shared with Hog Creek.

blocks.text: The second of the two creeks that meet to form the Ottawa River. Its mouth is at 40.7708852, -83.9557761 and it rises at 40.722274, -83.8979957. [verified] — [USGS GNIS](../../catalog/gnis-domestic-names-ohio.md), feature 1042627.
Its mouth coordinate is byte-identical to [Hog Creek](hog-creek.yml)'s mouth and to [the Ottawa River](ottawa-river.yml)'s source. [verified] — same source.

nodes.label: Maumee River Basin

blocks.text: The drainage basin that **almost all** of Allen County lies within — the largest watershed draining to the Great Lakes, discharging to Lake Erie at Toledo. 3,548 of the county's 3,552 census blocks and 102,107 of its 102,206 people are in the Great Lakes Region, across three subbasins: Auglaize `04100007` holds 3,200 blocks and Blanchard `04100008` holds 348. [verified] — [USGS Watershed Boundary Dataset](../../catalog/usgs-watershed-boundary.md), by block composition.

**This basin is not a hydrologic unit, which is why no code is recorded here.** The Maumee's drainage is seven subbasins — `04100003` St. Joseph through `04100009` Lower Maumee — and the next unit up that contains them, `041000` Western Lake Erie, also contains six that are nothing to do with the Maumee: Raisin, Sandusky, Huron and three more. [verified] — [USGS Watershed Boundary Dataset](../../catalog/usgs-watershed-boundary.md). So the honest answer to this node's genesis question about its own HUC is that it does not have one, and writing `0410` here would have named a basin four times too large.

**Its other genesis question is answered against it.** Part of Allen County does drain to the Ohio River: four blocks in [Auglaize Township](../place/auglaize-township.yml), 99 people, sit in [the Scioto basin](scioto-river-basin.yml). [verified] — same source. The corpus asserted the Lake Erie side for the whole county from genesis and flagged the southern townships as unchecked; checking them cost one query and moved 99 people to the Gulf of Mexico.

refusals: It is included at genesis for that reason: without it the trace from the Ottawa River runs to the Auglaize and stops in mid-air, and the corpus cannot say where its water goes.

properties.source: 41.0828261, -85.1321928 — the St. Joseph and St. Marys confluence, Fort Wayne.

blocks.text: The river Allen County's water reaches last before Lake Erie. It rises at 41.0828261, -85.1321928 — the confluence of the St. Joseph and St. Marys at Fort Wayne, Indiana — and discharges at 41.6994922, -83.4599325 at Toledo. [verified] — [USGS GNIS](../../catalog/gnis-domestic-names-ohio.md), feature 1084017.

The discharge coordinate is what makes the corpus's Lake Erie claim more than an assertion. Allen County's water leaves the county by the Auglaize, and the river the Auglaize joins ends at Toledo on Lake Erie rather than anywhere on the Ohio. [inference] — the coordinate is verified; that the Auglaize joins *this* river at Defiance is not established by a names file.

nodes.label: Ottawa River

properties.huc_code: 0410000703 Upper Ottawa River, 0410000705 Lower Ottawa River
properties.mouth: 40.9950509, -84.2413355, in Putnam County. Joins the Auglaize River. [inference]
properties.source: 40.7708852, -83.9557761 — the Hog Creek / Little Hog Creek confluence.

blocks.text: The stream that runs through Lima, and the county's principal watercourse. It begins at 40.7708852, -83.9557761 and discharges at 40.9950509, -84.2413355 in Putnam County. [verified] — [USGS GNIS](../../catalog/gnis-domestic-names-ohio.md), feature 1070882. That the discharge point is on the Auglaize remains [inference]: a names file gives a coordinate and never says what is at it.

**It does not begin east of the city; it begins at a confluence.** Its source coordinate is identical to the mouths GNIS records for [Hog Creek](hog-creek.yml) and [Little Hog Creek](little-hog-creek.yml), so the river's head is where those two creeks meet. [verified] — same source. The older name of the whole watercourse was Hog Creek, and the name now attaches to the upper tributary; GNIS is consistent with that and does not establish it. [inference]

**Allen County's own rows do not contain it.** GNIS files a stream under the county of its mouth, so the county's principal river is filed under Putnam and is absent from the 113 features listed for Allen. [verified] — same source.

The present name is shared with a larger, unrelated Ottawa River near Toledo — feature 1066879 in Lucas County against this one's 1070882. [verified] — same source. The collision is now resolvable by identifier rather than by care.

**Where its water goes is now sourced rather than assumed.** The river has two watersheds of its own — `0410000703` Upper Ottawa River and `0410000705` Lower Ottawa River — and both sit inside subbasin `04100007`, which is named for and drains to the [Auglaize](auglaize-river.yml). [verified] — [USGS Watershed Boundary Dataset](../../catalog/usgs-watershed-boundary.md). That settles the basin and not the confluence: the WBD says this water reaches the Auglaize and never says which stream it joins first. Those two Ottawa watersheds hold 47,578 of the county's people between them, 47 per cent, which is what it means to call this the county's principal watercourse.

Being the watercourse Lima grew on, it was also the receiving water for the refinery and the works — the environmental history of this stream and the industrial history of the city are the same subject. [inference]

refusals: The older name of the whole watercourse was Hog Creek, and the name now attaches to the upper tributary; GNIS is consistent with that and does not establish it.

blocks.text: The drainage basin of the Scioto River, which discharges to the Ohio River at Portsmouth and through it to the Gulf of Mexico. **Ninety-nine people in Allen County live in it.** [verified] — [USGS Watershed Boundary Dataset](../../catalog/usgs-watershed-boundary.md).

Four census blocks in [Auglaize Township](../place/auglaize-township.yml), at the county's south-east corner between 40.6487 and 40.7104 north, fall in hydrologic unit `05060001` — the Upper Scioto subbasin of the Ohio Region. Every other block in the county, 3,548 of 3,552, is in the Great Lakes Region and drains to [the Maumee basin](maumee-river-basin.yml). [verified] — same source, by block composition; all 3,552 blocks land in exactly one subbasin and their populations sum to the county's own enumeration of 102,206.

The subwatershed those four blocks sit in is `050600010101`, **Cottonwood Ditch** — a headwater of the Scioto rising in Auglaize Township. [verified] — same source. It is the only named feature on the Ohio River side of the divide in this county.

The county's elected chief law enforcement officer, one of the separately elected county offices Ohio law establishes for every county. [inference] The sheriff runs the county jail and serves process in addition to policing the unincorporated area.

**Its line of holders is complete.** Thirty-nine tenures run from Henry Lippencott in 1831 to the present holder, with every term's end year equal to the next term's start year and no holder recorded twice in succession. [verified] — [Allen County Sheriff's Office past-sheriffs roster](../../catalog/acso-past-sheriffs.md); the continuity was checked across all thirty-nine entries rather than assumed, and is now checked by [`crates/succession`](../../../crates/succession/) on every test run rather than by hand.

Two features of the line are worth knowing before computing on it. John Keller held the office in 1835–1839 and again in 1843–1845, so the corpus carries one person and two tenures with `term_number` set. [verified] And the roster's ranges are year-only, so consecutive tenures share a boundary year; read as day-precision intervals every adjacent pair overlaps, and none of those overlaps is real.
The elected chief executive of the [City of Lima](../jurisdiction/city-of-lima.yml). [inference]
A private liberal arts university at [Bluffton](../place/bluffton.yml), with a Mennonite affiliation reflecting the Swiss Mennonite settlement of that part of the county. [inference]

**Its residential population is now a measured number.** Census block `390030101001002` holds 398 people in 2 housing units — a population living almost entirely outside housing, which is what a campus looks like in the block file. The county's address file puts Ropp Hall 0.02 miles from that block's internal point, with Bren Dell Hall, College Hall and Musselman Library inside 0.15. [verified] — [TIGERweb](../../catalog/tigerweb-census2020.md) block layer and [Allen County GIS](../../catalog/allen-county-gis-downloads.md). The 398 are students in residence on census day; they are not the university's enrolment, and the campus is not necessarily one block. [inference]

That block is in [Bluffton](../place/bluffton.yml) village, which settles by assignment rather than by inference where the university sits. [verified] — [2020 Census Block Assignment Files](../../catalog/census-block-assignment-2020.md).

The locomotive builder that made Lima's name in railroading. It began as a machine shop building the geared Shay locomotive under Ephraim Shay's patent — a design for logging and industrial railways that could work steep, rough, temporary track that a conventional rod locomotive could not. [inference]

It later became one of the three major American builders of mainline steam, and is associated with the "Super Power" concept — a design direction emphasising boiler capacity and free steaming that the company introduced in the mid-1920s. [inference]

The Standard Oil subsidiary that built and operated [the Lima refinery](../site/lima-refinery.yml) — the corporate name attached to the county's longest-running industrial installation, and the first link in an ownership chain the refinery node has asked for since genesis. [verified] — [A Standard History of Allen County, 1921](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md).

**It appears in the record as the buyer, not as Standard.** When Standard Oil resolved in 1886 to put a refinery in north-west Ohio, the committee that toured the candidate sites was Frank Rockefeller, the director F. B. Squiers, and **Keith, "an attorney for the Solar Refining Company"** — and the 151 acres of the Hover farm were contracted "to the Solar Refining Company". So the entity that dealt with the landowner, took the deed and took possession was Solar, with Standard's officers making the decision. [verified] — same source. That distinction is why [Standard Oil](standard-oil.yml) and this node are separate: one chose, the other bought.

Thirty-five years later the 1921 historian's summary of what the boom left is one clause: "About all that is left is the Solar refinery and the different companies dealing in oil commodities." [verified] — same source. The refinery had already outlasted the field that justified it, which is the fact [the boom's](../period/lima-oil-boom.yml) end bound is really about.

In 1918 it was one of nine Lima industrial firms that agreed to meet half the cost of equipping a machine shop at South High School, alongside Lima Locomotive Works and the Ohio Steel Foundry. [verified] — same source. It is also a corporate life member of the Lima Hospital Society, with the Buckeye Pipe Line Company, the Ohio Oil Company, the Lima Natural Gas Company and the Manhattan Oil Company. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1906](../../catalog/miller-allen-county-1906.md).

The company that industrialized the Lima oil field after the 1885 strike. Standard Oil bought into the field, built refining capacity at Lima, and solved the problem that had made Lima crude nearly worthless — its high sulphur content, which fouled refining and gave the product the name "sour crude" — by acquiring a desulphurization process. [inference]

It matters to this corpus as the mechanism by which a local discovery became a national one. The strike made oil available; Standard made it saleable, and in doing so attached this county to a national industrial economy in a way its agriculture never had. [inference]

**The Standard entity at Lima was the [Solar Refining Company](solar-refining-company.yml)**, and the corpus can now date its arrival: in 1886 a Standard committee — Frank Rockefeller, the director F. B. Squiers and Solar's attorney Keith — chose 151 acres in [Shawnee Township](../place/shawnee-township.yml) for [the refinery](../site/lima-refinery.yml) over Findlay and Toledo. [verified] — [A Standard History of Allen County, 1921](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md). Standard "at once established headquarters" at Lima and was still operating there in 1921. [verified] — same source. It "cornered the Lima oil fields and went into the producing business, building the Chicago pipe line and becoming master of the oil supply of the world" — the 1921 historian's phrasing, and this corpus records it as his. [verified] — same source.

Two more of its Lima entities are named in the record: the **Buckeye Pipe Line Company** and the **Ohio Oil Company**, which with Solar and the independent Manhattan Oil Company appear together as corporate subscribers to the Lima Hospital Society. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1906](../../catalog/miller-allen-county-1906.md).

properties.character: Water transport as the organizing fact of the county's west, and a divided county economy. [inference]

blocks.text: The span in which [the Miami and Erie Canal](../site/miami-and-erie-canal.yml) was the organizing transport fact of western Allen County — roughly the 1840s to the end of the nineteenth century, when rail had comprehensively displaced it. [inference]

Its character is a geographic asymmetry rather than a countywide condition, and that is the reason it is worth naming as a period at all. The canal ran through the county's western edge and made [Delphos](../place/delphos.yml) and Spencerville into places; it did not touch Lima, which grew instead around a railway junction. So for several decades the county had two economies oriented to two different transport systems, and its later concentration on Lima is partly the story of one of them winning. [inference]

**The opening bound is now sourced and the corpus's guess was right.** The Miami extension was formally opened in June 1845, and traffic was moving at Spencerville by 1844. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md). 1845 was written here as "the corpus's rough placement" and is the date the state used.

**The closing bound now has an argument, and it moves.** The railways reached this county while the canal was still young: the Ohio & Indiana opened Crestline to Fort Wayne in 1854 and was consolidated into the Pennsylvania system in 1856; the Dayton & Michigan was chartered in 1856-57 and **completed through Allen County in 1858**. [verified] — same source. A canal whose parallel railway is finished thirteen years after it opens did not organize the county's west until 1900. [inference] The end bound is left at 1900 for now because "displaced" and "abandoned" are different dates and this corpus has argued neither.

nodes.label: Deindustrialization

properties.character: Contraction of manufacturing employment and sustained population loss concentrated in the county seat. The population half is verified; the manufacturing half is not. [inference]

blocks.text: The span from roughly 1970 in which the county's manufacturing employment contracted and [Lima](../place/lima.yml) entered the sustained population decline it is still in. [inference]

**There was a reversal, and this node said there was none.** Between 1970 and 1980 the county *grew*, from 111,144 to **112,241** — its highest count ever — before falling to 109,755 in 1990 and 108,464 in 2000. [verified] — [1990 Census, Population and Housing Unit Counts, Ohio](../../catalog/census-cph-2-37-ohio.md), Table 3. This node has said since genesis that there was "no reversal at any measured point", and that was true of the corpus's data and false of the county: every figure it held began at 1970 or later, so the one decade that rose was the one decade outside the window. **The county's peak is 1980.** See [the 1940–1990 series](../measure/allen-county-population-1940-1990.yml).

The period keeps its name and its subject and its start moves to what the record shows: the county's population turned in the 1970s and fell from 1980. [inference] Whether manufacturing employment turned earlier is still unmeasured here, and it is the thing the period is named for.

**The decline itself is demonstrated rather than asserted.** Allen County counted 111,144 at the 1970 census and 100,866 at the 2024 estimate — a loss of 10,278 people, or 9.2%, across five decades: 111,144 (1970), 108,464 (2000), 106,331 (2010), 102,217 (2020), 100,866 (2024). [verified] — see [1970](../measure/allen-county-population-1970.yml), [2000](../measure/allen-county-population-2000.yml), [2010](../measure/allen-county-population-2010.yml), [2020](../measure/allen-county-population-2020.yml) and [2024](../measure/allen-county-population-2024.yml). The arithmetic is this corpus's; every input is a Census figure.

**The concentration is now evidenced too, over one decade.** This node carries a `concentrated-in` edge to Lima, and between 2000 and 2010 Lima fell 3.8% while the balance of Allen County — everything outside every incorporated place — fell 1.5%, from 50,809 to 50,048. [verified] — [Census Intercensal Estimates, 2000–2010](../../catalog/census-intercensal-2000-2010.md). Lima declined about two and a half times as fast as the rest of the county. [inference]

**The county's 1970 peak is no longer an artefact of where the data began.** The series now runs 578 in 1830 through 47,976 in 1900 and 68,203 in 1920 to 111,144 in 1970, and every decade of it rises. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1906](../../catalog/miller-allen-county-1906.md) and [A Standard History of Allen County, 1921](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md); see [the county series](../measure/allen-county-population-1830-1900.yml). Four counts are still missing, 1930 to 1960, and nothing in ninety years of ascent suggests a reversal inside them. [inference] For the county, this node's start date is now argued rather than assumed.

**For Lima the 1970 date is supported after all, and by a wide margin.** The city was **53,734 in 1970**, 47,827 in 1980, 45,549 in 1990 and 40,307 in 2000. [verified] — [Lima 1970–1990](../measure/lima-population-1970-1990.yml). One phase ago this node reasoned from 41,306 in 1920 against 40,307 in 2000 that "eighty years net to roughly nothing" and the peak was unlocatable. There was a peak and the corpus had drawn a chord across it. The city rose thirty per cent above its 1920 count by 1970 and has fallen at every count since.

**The corporation's boundary moved underneath the city's counts.** Between 1980 and 1990 Lima annexed ground from American, Bath and Shawnee townships. [verified] — [1990 Census, Population and Housing Unit Counts, Ohio](../../catalog/census-cph-2-37-ohio.md), Geographic Change Notes. So the fall from 47,827 to 45,549 happened while the corporation was growing, and understates the decline inside the old line. [inference] This is the first annexation event the corpus has held against a caveat it has carried since genesis.

**The mechanism, for the first time.** Across the four full years 2021 to 2024 the county lost 1,271 people: **506 to natural decrease and 793 to net migration**, with a residual of 28. [verified] — [natural change](../measure/allen-county-natural-change-2021-2024.yml) and [net migration](../measure/allen-county-net-migration-2021-2024.yml), both from the same Population Estimates file this node has cited since its second phase. More people leave than arrive, and more die than are born, and the first is the larger of the two.

**The decline is broad and uneven.** Between the 2020 estimates base and 2024, eleven of the county's thirteen civil subdivisions lost population. Lima lost most in absolute terms — 841 of a county loss of 1,351 — and the only two that grew were Auglaize township, by 55, and Marion township, by 102, at the county's south-eastern and Delphos ends. [verified] — [Census Population Estimates](../../catalog/census-popest-2024.md), sub-county file. So this is not a city emptying into its own suburbs: the suburban ring is shrinking too, slower. [inference]

refusals: **What the evidence does not establish, stated plainly.** It does not establish that Lima peaked in 1970 rather than earlier: 1970 is the first of the three federal counts the corpus holds for the city, and a series that begins at its own first observation cannot show that the first observation was a peak.

It does not establish anything about *manufacturing employment*, which is the mechanism this period is named for and which the corpus does not measure at all: every figure here is population, and population decline is a consequence being read back as evidence for a cause.
It does not establish that either mechanism reaches back before 2020.

It does not establish that the decline has ended: fifteen people on 100,851 is far inside what a modelled estimate can resolve, one year is not a direction, and the same programme revises its own earlier years with every vintage.

properties.character: A local discovery converted into national industry, and the county's shift from agriculture to manufacturing. [inference]

blocks.text: The span opened by [the 1885 strike](../event/lima-oil-strike.yml), in which the Lima–Indiana field made this county a centre of national petroleum production and Lima an industrial city. [inference]

Its character is the attachment of a local agricultural economy to national capital. The refinery, the growth of Lima's population, and much of the built fabric of the city date from it. [inference] The field's dominance was relatively brief — it was displaced as new fields opened elsewhere — but the refining capacity it justified is still operating, which is why the period's most durable legacy is [a site](../site/lima-refinery.yml) rather than an industry. [inference]

**The start bound is now supported from the other side.** The 1885 county history, printed as the boom began, treats the county's petroleum as prospective — "a subject for the enterprise of the future" — while cataloguing everything else in Lima to the dollar. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md). A source that would have reported the field and does not is a lower bound on the field. [inference]

**The start bound is now a date: May 9, 1885.** [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1906](../../catalog/miller-allen-county-1906.md). It is also, on the same source, a slightly later date in substance — the first *persistent* production came from the second well that autumn, the pioneer having broken. [inference]

**The boom is now measurable and the measure is large.** Allen County gained 9,330 people between 1880 and 1890 — **29.7 per cent, the largest decennial gain in its history** — and Lima "doubled her population" in the same decade, going from 7,567 to 21,723 by 1900. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1906](../../catalog/miller-allen-county-1906.md); see [the county series](../measure/allen-county-population-1830-1900.yml) and [Lima's](../measure/lima-population-1880-1920.yml). The 1906 compilers attribute the increase to the discovery without qualification, and they were living in the town when it happened.

**And the end bound has a shape at last, though not a date.** By 1920 Lima had reached 41,306 and by 1921 the whole residue of the field was, in the later historian's words, "the Solar refinery and the different companies dealing in oil commodities", with "little oil now being pumped in Allen County". [verified] — [A Standard History of Allen County, 1921](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md). So the *field* was substantially finished before 1921 while the *city* kept growing — which is why this period's legacy is a site rather than an industry, and why 1910 as a placeholder is defensible for production and wrong for consequence. [inference]

The Lima businessman whose drilling produced the 1885 strike that opened the Lima oil field. [inference] He was drilling for natural gas, on the pattern of the Findlay gas boom to the north, and struck oil instead. [inference]

**His other business interests are now on record, and they are most of industrial Lima.** [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md), printed the year of the strike and therefore describing him entirely as he was before it:

The county itself, as ground rather than as government: 402.545 square miles of land and 4.306 square miles of water in the northwest quarter of Ohio, with an internal point at 40.771627, -84.106103. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md).

The land is glacial till plain, flat and poorly drained, and its northern reach lay within the Great Black Swamp until nineteenth-century drainage. [inference] That flatness is the reason the county's transport history runs through a canal and then a railway junction rather than through a river port: its streams drain north and west to the Auglaize and the Maumee and were never navigable here.

**It is three places.** Lima holds 35,531 people; the three townships wrapped around it — [American](american-township.yml) 14,571, [Shawnee](shawnee-township.yml) 12,509 and [Bath](bath-township.yml) 9,399 — hold 36,479 between them, more than the city; and the other nine townships hold about thirty thousand across roughly five hundred square miles. [verified] — [Census Population Estimates](../../catalog/census-popest-2024.md), sub-county file. That suburban middle is largely outside any municipality: Shawnee Township contains no incorporated place at all. [verified] — same source.

A township of 33.315 square miles about 9 miles west of the county's centre, internal point 40.734865, -84.272548. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md), Ohio county subdivisions.

Its population was 2,070 at the 2020 estimates base and 2,049 in 2024. [verified] — [Census Population Estimates](../../catalog/census-popest-2024.md), sub-county file. Its population fell by 21 over those four years, as all but two of the county's subdivisions did.
It contains no incorporated place; all of it is unincorporated. [verified] — same source, which lists no place within this township.

**No school district is named for it and three divide it**: 1,072 of its people are in [Spencerville Local](../jurisdiction/spencerville-local-school-district.yml), 665 in [Shawnee Local](../jurisdiction/shawnee-local-school-district.yml) and 324 in [Elida Local](../jurisdiction/elida-local-school-district.yml). [verified] — [2020 Census Block Assignment Files](../../catalog/census-block-assignment-2020.md) crossed with [TIGERweb](../../catalog/tigerweb-census2020.md) block geography. A township with no village and no district of its own has no institution that takes its name as a whole, which is worth knowing before reading anything into how little is written about it.

**Erected in 1830 by the commissioners of Mercer County** — the earliest township organization recorded in this county, and it happened two years before Allen County had a board of its own, while Allen was attached to Mercer for judicial purposes. Thirteen electors lived in it and twelve of them came to the organizing meeting; Samuel Baxter was chosen clerk and Daniel Hoak justice of the peace. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md).

**It is named for Fort Amanda**, built here in 1812 by Col. Poague's command and named for the colonel's wife. [verified] — same source. In the [reorganization of 1848](../event/reorganization-of-1848.yml) it lost sections 7 and 18 to [Spencer](spencer-township.yml) and was recomposed from the south half of Marion and its own north half. [verified] — same source.
A township of 24.017 square miles wrapping the west and north of Lima, internal point 40.769378, -84.17822. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md).

It is the most populous township in the county outside Lima itself, and the Census Bureau's "balance of American township" figure — the township minus the incorporated villages inside it — is the larger part of that. [verified] — [Census Population Estimates](../../catalog/census-popest-2024.md), sub-county file. Its population was 14,571 at the 2020 estimates base and 14,445 in 2024 — **the most populous civil subdivision in the county after Lima**, and 12,541 of the 2024 figure is the balance outside [Elida](elida.yml), the one village in it. [verified] — same source.

**Neither the refinery nor the tank plant is here.** This node claimed both stand on or near its boundary with Lima, and therefore that this township holds most of the county's heavy industry. Both are in [Shawnee Township](shawnee-township.yml), south of Lima; this township wraps Lima's west and north. [verified] — [Allen County GIS](../../catalog/allen-county-gis-downloads.md) and [TIGERweb](../../catalog/tigerweb-census2020.md), agreeing independently on both points. The claim is withdrawn entire rather than narrowed: it named two sites and was wrong about both.
It does hold a fifth of [census tract 39003010300](../division/census-tract-39003010300.yml) — 13,403,443 square metres and 408 people. [verified] — same source, block composition.

**This township was called German until some time after 1885.** The commissioners' act of December 6, 1831 established it "under the name German", over the territory running west from Section 3, Town 3, Range 6 to the old Amanda line. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md). That book's German Township "forms the geographical centre of the county", takes the Ottawa River in from [Shawnee](shawnee-township.yml) at Section 33, and passes it by Allentown and [Elida](elida.yml) into [Sugar Creek](sugar-creek-township.yml) — which is this township and no other, since Elida is in it and in nothing else. [inference] Its erection date therefore belongs here, and it makes this the third township the county had.

In 1848 it lost its north tier of sections to Sugar Creek and kept its name; in 1857 it gave 1,040 acres to Ottawa Township. [verified] — same source, and [A Standard History of Allen County, 1921](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md) independently, giving the same acreage thirty-six years later.

**The name changed on August 16, 1918, and the reason was the war.** The citizens of German Township petitioned, and the Allen County commissioners acted — the same instrument that erected the county's townships and incorporated its villages. Article II of the petition says only "that good cause is shown"; the 1921 historian reads it plainly — "'good cause' means patriotism" — and sets it in its moment: "The name German had come into disfavor when the German nation changed its attitude toward the rest of the world. School books were undergoing changes at the time, and business concerns bearing the name German were eliminating the offensive designation, and the people of German Township were caught in the wave of popular sentiment." [verified] — [A Standard History of Allen County, 1921](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md), which is a single witness read once for this date.

**The same page records the dissent**, three years after the fact: "there are residents of the township who a little later on would not have voted for the change, because of sacred associations in early history. They do not hold the German people responsible for the conduct of some of their leaders." [verified] — same source. The corpus had declined to assert the obvious motive; the motive is confirmed, and so is that it was contested at the time.

A township of 35.99 square miles about 11 miles south-east of the county's centre, internal point 40.695518, -83.928053. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md), Ohio county subdivisions.

Its population was 2,764 at the 2020 estimates base and 2,819 in 2024. [verified] — [Census Population Estimates](../../catalog/census-popest-2024.md), sub-county file. It is one of only two subdivisions in the county that grew over those four years, by 55.

It contains [Harrod](harrod.yml) [verified] — same source, which reports it as a place within this township — and also [Westminster](westminster.yml), a census designated place of 406 that the sub-county file does not list because it has no government. [verified] — [2020 Census Block Assignment Files](../../catalog/census-block-assignment-2020.md).

Its schools are split: 2,740 of its people are in [Allen East Local](../jurisdiction/allen-east-local-school-district.yml) and 17, on two blocks at the south-east corner, in Auglaize County's [Waynesfield-Goshen](../jurisdiction/waynesfield-goshen-local-school-district.yml). [verified] — same source, crossed with [TIGERweb](../../catalog/tigerweb-census2020.md) block geography.

**The continental divide runs through it.** Four of its census blocks — 99 people and 43 housing units, along the county's eastern edge between 40.6487 and 40.7104 north — are in [the Scioto basin](../natural-feature/scioto-river-basin.yml) and drain to the Ohio River and the Gulf of Mexico. They are the only ground in Allen County that does. [verified] — [USGS Watershed Boundary Dataset](../../catalog/usgs-watershed-boundary.md), by block composition.

**Established March 5, 1832 by order of the commissioners of Allen County** — the first township the county's own board created from nothing rather than inherited. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md).

**A township named Scioto was disestablished into it in December 1832** and attached to Auglaize "for judicial purposes"; until [Perry](perry-township.yml) was established in December 1833 its twelve eastern sections were part of this township. [verified] — same source. The county has carried no Scioto township since, and this township is still where [its Gulf-side ground](../natural-feature/scioto-river-basin.yml) lies — the only part of Allen County that drains to the Ohio.

**The later history says Scioto is unexplained; the earlier one explains it.** In 1921 Rusler writes that "when Allen County was organized in 1831, its four townships were Amanda, Bath, Jackson and Scioto; in 1832 there was a German but no Scioto and no explanation is offered about it." [verified] — [A Standard History of Allen County, 1921](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md). The explanation is in the book on the shelf beside it: the commissioners disestablished Scioto in December 1832 and attached its district to this township for judicial purposes. The corpus's older source answers its newer source's stated gap — which is the argument for holding both.

Wood, John Schrouf and James Daniels as justices. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md). The [Village of Beaverdam](../jurisdiction/village-of-beaverdam.yml) was incorporated twenty-five years later, in 1878.

The county's page gives 1853 and no name; this source gives the name, and the two agree on the year against an OCR reading of 1858 in the other scan — see [two scans of one book](../../decisions/two-scans-of-one-book.yml), where an unrelated source settling a scanning dispute is the case the rule was written for.

blocks.text: A village of 3.652 square miles in the county's north, internal point 40.892048, -83.887793. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md).

It is the seat of Bluffton University and has a Swiss Mennonite settlement history that distinguishes it from the rest of the county. [inference] **It was originally known as Shannon.** [verified] — [Allen County](../../catalog/allen-county-official-site.md), cities and villages page, which also names [Bluffton University](../organization/bluffton-university.yml) here and its Mennonite affiliation.

[verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md), both scans agreeing. At 1837 it is the county's second-oldest platted town after [Lima](lima.yml), and it was called something else for the first thirty-five years of that.

A village of 0.277 square miles in [Monroe Township](monroe-township.yml), about 4 miles north of the county's centre, internal point 40.830753, -84.084489. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md), Ohio places.

**It was platted in 1848 by Jacob Miller**, on Sections 29, 30, 31 and 32 of [Monroe Township](monroe-township.yml), running east from the Brenneman farm and lying mainly west of the Perrysburg Road at its crossing with the Bucyrus Road. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md). The county's own page gives 1848 without a founder; this is a second source arriving at the same year by a different route, seventy years earlier.

**The corporation dates from April 12, 1875**, twenty-seven years after the plat: "the village lay dormant awaiting developments until April 12, 1875, when it was organized and it still maintains a corporate existence." [verified] — [A Standard History of Allen County, 1921](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md). A single witness read once, and the only incorporation date the corpus has for this village.

blocks.text: A city of 3.322 square miles on the county's western edge, internal point 40.846581, -84.336474. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md).

Delphos straddles the Allen–Van Wert county line, and the Census Bureau's Allen County rows record it as `Delphos city (pt.)` for exactly that reason: the 3,941 counted there in the 2020 estimates base is the Allen County portion, not the city. [verified] — [Census Population Estimates](../../catalog/census-popest-2024.md). Any figure for Delphos taken from an Allen County table and reported as the city's population understates it. Its edge to the county is `partially-within` for the same reason, matching the qualification [the Village of Bluffton](../jurisdiction/village-of-bluffton.yml) already carries.

The city grew as a port on the Miami and Erie Canal, which is why it sits on the county edge rather than on any natural centre. [inference] See [the Miami and Erie Canal](../site/miami-and-erie-canal.yml). **It was four towns before it was one.** The county records Delphos as originally Howard, Section Ten, West Bredeick and East Bredeick, merged into a single town in 1851. [verified] — [Allen County](../../catalog/allen-county-official-site.md), cities and villages page. That is the only municipality in the county the source describes as made rather than founded, and it is a different kind of origin from a platted town site: four settlements with four names, none of which survives on the map.

**The merged town was incorporated by an act of February 7, 1851**, and held its first election on March 3, returning Lester Bliss as mayor and Smith Talbott as recorder. The corporation spent $80.67 in its first year. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md), both scans agreeing on the act's date. That puts a day on the year [the county's own page](../../catalog/allen-county-official-site.md) gives for the merger, from a source that had never seen it.

**Section Ten was a place before it was a name.** The tract was the Ten-Mile Woods: in 1834 William Brady and William Scott cut a road from the Auglaize River through it to Van Wert and "not even one cabin was to be seen in all that distance". [verified] — same source. The town's first newspaper, in 1848, was still called the *Section Ten Budget*.

[verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md). Griffith John is the same man who petitioned the commissioners in March 1833 to enlarge German Township and who assessed its district in 1846: the village was laid out by the township's own long-standing figure, on ground he had spent twenty years enlarging. [verified] — same source.

**It is named for the founder's brother.** "Griffith John was its founder, and it bears the name of his brother Elida John who never lived in the community." [verified] — [A Standard History of Allen County, 1921](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md), which also confirms 1852 and the 1878 incorporation. That is a single witness read once, and it is the only etymology the corpus has for this village; the commonly repeated alternative — that Elida is a contraction of two women's names — appears in no source held here.

[inference] As a CDP it is a statistical outline and not a boundary anyone is governed by, and it does not reach the tank plant a mile and a half north of its internal point — the plant is in Shawnee Township and in no place at all. [verified] — same source, which names Welsh families among the township's farmers. The local account of a Welsh settlement here is therefore not folklore.

**The Harrod was William Harrod**, born in Knox County, Ohio on October 4, 1819, of Pennsylvania stock and from a family among Knox County's early pioneers. He settled on the land in 1841 and still occupied it in 1885; his son J. M. Harrod was born in [Auglaize Township](auglaize-township.yml) on March 7, 1852 and farmed there, with the post office already carrying the family name. A township of 35.719 square miles about 10 miles east of the county's centre, internal point 40.781058, -83.920597. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md), Ohio county subdivisions.

Wood and Samuel Stewart first sat. **The village is one voting precinct, exactly.** Precinct `LAFAYETTE` holds 406 people and 175 housing units, and every block in it is in the village and every block of the village is in it. Weyer**, in Section 28 of [Jackson Township](jackson-township.yml), laid out in regular blocks north of Sugar Street with Weyer's own western and southern additions around it. **The commissioners granted authority to organize the village on September 3, 1867**, on M. [verified] — same source, county subdivision file.

**It tripled after the oil, peaked around 1970 and has lost a third of itself since.** 7,567 in 1880, 21,723 in 1900, 41,306 in 1920, **53,734 in 1970**, 47,827 in 1980, 45,549 in 1990, 40,307 in 2000, 35,579 in 2020. The corpus wrote here one phase ago that the city "was already at its 2000 size before the First World War ended", reasoning from the 1920 and 2000 figures alone. Two points that happen to be level are not a plateau: between them the city grew by a third and then lost it.

Lima is the county's industrial centre and the reason its history is not an agricultural one: the 1885 oil strike, the locomotive works, and the tank plant are all here or on its edge. [inference] Its population has been falling since the 1970s and continues to fall — see [Lima population, 2020](../measure/lima-population-2020.yml) and [Lima population, 2024](../measure/lima-population-2024.yml).

[verified] — [2020 Census Block Assignment Files](../../catalog/census-block-assignment-2020.md) crossed with [TIGERweb](../../catalog/tigerweb-census2020.md) block geography, block by block. **Founded in 1831**, and the county seat. [verified] — [Allen County](../../catalog/allen-county-official-site.md), cities and villages page — which puts it on Interstate 75 about 72 miles north of Dayton and 78 south of Toledo, the county's own way of saying where it is.

**It is also where the county's minority vote lives, and where it is shrinking fastest.** Eleven of Allen County's 88 precincts went to Biden in 2020 and ten of them are here; the county as a whole went 69 to 29 the other way. [verified] — [OpenElections](../../catalog/openelections-ohio.md). The city holds a third of the county's people, most of its density, five school districts and 23 of its 88 precincts, and on every one of those measures it is the part that does not resemble the rest.

Between 2016 and 2020 its 23 precincts moved toward the Republicans by a mean of **3.2 points** while the county's other 65 moved 1.6 — the city drifting right about twice as fast as the ground around it, from a much more Democratic starting point. [verified] — same source, computed across three general elections. So the county's political division is narrowing from the city's side, which is the opposite of the direction its [population decline](../period/deindustrialization.yml) runs.

A township of 42.371 square miles about 10 miles west of the county's centre, internal point 40.81041, -84.292789. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md), Ohio county subdivisions.

[verified] — same source.

A township of 41.648 square miles about 11 miles north-east of the county's centre, internal point 40.869365, -83.936562. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md), Ohio county subdivisions.

Its population was 5,889 at the 2020 estimates base and 5,775 in 2024. [verified] — [Census Population Estimates](../../catalog/census-popest-2024.md), sub-county file. Its population fell by 114 over those four years, as all but two of the county's subdivisions did.
It contains [Beaverdam](beaverdam.yml) and [Bluffton](bluffton.yml). [verified] — same source, which reports them as places within this township.

**Organized in 1835 as a township of Putnam County**, on the petition of David Miller and others, with Henry Shank and Daniel Goble the first justices and Henry Carter the first constable. **It was not in Allen County until 1848**, when the [reorganization](../event/reorganization-of-1848.yml) added Riley Township's south tier to it. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md).

**It is named for Richland County, Ohio.** Henry Carter's reminiscence, recorded in 1885, credits David Miller — a shoemaker "just in from Richland County" — with pushing the new township through and giving it his former county's name. [verified] — same source. That is a settler's recollection of fifty years earlier, not a record entry, and it is the only name origin in the county that comes with the person who chose it.
A township of 28.97 square miles immediately south and west of Lima, internal point 40.691353, -84.170464. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md).

**Its name was chosen for that reason and the record says so.** The commissioners, in session December 1, 1834, granted the petition of the people of Shawnee to set Township 4, Range 6 off from the Hog Creek Reservation "under the name of its original inhabitants"; the first meeting was held on December 13 in Ezekiel Hover's log house, and the list of voters ran to twelve names. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md). The township was cut twice afterwards: its south tier went to the new county of Auglaize in 1848, and the north-east quarter of Section 1 to Ottawa Township in May 1857. [verified] — same source. The name is the clearest surviving toponymic trace in the county's civil geography of the people who were removed from it — and the book that records the naming introduces them as "sanguinary savages", which is a fact about the source and not about them. See [the Ottawa removal](../event/ottawa-removal.yml). With 12,509 people at the 2020 estimates base and 12,490 in 2024 it is the county's second most populous civil subdivision after Lima — and it **contains no incorporated place at all**. [verified] — [Census Population Estimates](../../catalog/census-popest-2024.md), sub-county file, which lists no place row under this township. Twelve and a half thousand people live here under township government and no municipal one.

**It holds the county's heavy industry**, which the corpus attributed to Lima at genesis and to [American Township](american-township.yml) alongside it. Both the [refinery](../site/lima-refinery.yml) and the [tank plant](../site/lima-army-tank-plant.yml) stand on unincorporated ground in this township, with Lima postal addresses and no municipality. [verified] — [Allen County GIS](../../catalog/allen-county-gis-downloads.md) and [TIGERweb](../../catalog/tigerweb-census2020.md).

That is a fact about tax base and authority as much as geography: the two largest industrial installations in the county are outside every municipality that could levy on them, and the township is the government whose ground they sit on. [inference]

A township of 23.308 square miles about 14 miles west of the county's centre, internal point 40.732439, -84.371928. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md), Ohio county subdivisions.

Its population was 3,058 at the 2020 estimates base and 2,998 in 2024. [verified] — [Census Population Estimates](../../catalog/census-popest-2024.md), sub-county file. Its population fell by 60 over those four years, as all but two of the county's subdivisions did.
It contains [Spencerville](spencerville.yml). [verified] — same source, which reports it as a place within this township.

**The county's youngest township, created February 28, 1848** — it did not exist before the [reorganization](../event/reorganization-of-1848.yml), which took the north-east quarter of Salem and the east half of Jennings **from Van Wert County**, added sections 7 and 18 of [Amanda](amanda-township.yml), and set the whole off under a new name. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md).

Its two parent townships have dates of their own: Jennings was laid off June 2, 1834 and organized at Benjamin Griffin's house on June 21; Salem was established in December 1836 and organized at Michael Tippe's house in January 1837, set off from the older township of Wayne. [verified] — same source.

**It is named for Col. Spencer**, a member of the State Board of Public Works in 1848 and an ardent supporter of canal building — which is why the county's canal township carries a canal commissioner's name. [verified] — same source. See [the Miami and Erie Canal](../site/miami-and-erie-canal.yml), whose lock is in section 36 of this township. Charles C. Marshall was justice of the peace at organization.

A village of 0.965 square miles in [Spencer Township](spencer-township.yml), about 14 miles west of the county's centre, internal point 40.707965, -84.353159. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md), Ohio places.

Its population was 2,205 at the 2020 estimates base and 2,164 in 2024. [verified] — [Census Population Estimates](../../catalog/census-popest-2024.md), sub-county file. It lost 41 people over those four years.

**All of it is in Allen County.** The same file marks a place that crosses a county line with `(pt.)` and marks this one plainly, which is what separates it from [Bluffton](bluffton.yml) and [Delphos](delphos.yml). [verified] — same source.

**Founded in 1844 on the banks of the [Miami and Erie Canal](../site/miami-and-erie-canal.yml).** [verified] — [Allen County](../../catalog/allen-county-official-site.md), cities and villages page. That verifies for this village what the canal node had only inferred about the two canal towns, and it dates the settlement to the canal's own working decade.

**It was laid out about 1844-45 for Tyler, McConnell and Conover of Dayton**, who bought 350 acres and built a mill at the upper canal lock. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md), quoting Dr. Campbell's 1880 reminiscence. Speculators from Dayton buying at a lock the year the canal opened is what a canal town's founding looks like from the inside.

**The name is [Spencer Township's](spencer-township.yml), and that is Col. Spencer** of the State Board of Public Works in 1848, "an ardent supporter of canal building enterprises". [verified] — same source. The canal town is named, at one remove, for a canal commissioner.

**A village died to make it.** "The old village of Hartford ceased to exist upon the founding of Spencerville, to which location many of the Hartford people came to reside" — it had two physicians practising by 1836. [verified] — same source, though only one of the two scans carries the passage legibly; see [two scans of one book](../../decisions/two-scans-of-one-book.yml).

**[The corporation](../jurisdiction/village-of-spencerville.yml) dates from an act of 1867**, twenty-three years after the settlement. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md).

The **smallest of the county's thirteen civil subdivisions by population** and among its smallest by area — 24.094 square miles, internal point 40.824171, -84.173843. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md). Its 2020 estimates base was 1,226 and its 2024 estimate 1,197, a twelfth of American Township's on comparable ground, and it contains no incorporated place. [verified] — [Census Population Estimates](../../catalog/census-popest-2024.md), sub-county file.

It contains one settlement, [Gomer](gomer.yml), whose 345 people are 28 per cent of the township — a census designated place, so the claim above that it holds no *incorporated* place still stands. [verified] — [2020 Census Block Assignment Files](../../catalog/census-block-assignment-2020.md). It is also one of only two townships in the county that a single school district covers entire; every block of it is in [Elida Local](../jurisdiction/elida-local-school-district.yml), a district named for a village three miles south of this township and not in it. [verified] — same source, crossed with [TIGERweb](../../catalog/tigerweb-census2020.md) block geography.

**It was Putnam County's before it was Allen's.** The township was set off in 1831 as a division of Putnam County, then Congressional Township 2, Range 6, with James Porter, Daniel Gray and William Turner as its first trustees. Its present shape dates from the [reorganization of 1848](../event/reorganization-of-1848.yml), which joined the north tier of German Township — now [American](american-township.yml) — to the south half of the old township and organized the two as Sugar Creek. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md).

**It is named for its sugar maple groves**, whose number and productiveness the 1885 compiler gives as the origin, adding that the Shawnee took their year's supply of maple sugar from this ground. [verified] — same source.

An unincorporated community of 1.821 square miles in the south-east of the county, internal point 40.701038, -83.975081, with 406 people at the 2020 census. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md), where it is listed as `Westminster CDP`, and [TIGERweb](../../catalog/tigerweb-census2020.md) for the count.

It lies wholly within [Auglaize Township](auglaize-township.yml) — all fourteen of its census blocks do — and holds 15 per cent of that township's 2,757 people. [verified] — [2020 Census Block Assignment Files](../../catalog/census-block-assignment-2020.md) crossed with TIGERweb block geography. The generous test that county subdivisions merely *intersecting* it returns two townships, Auglaize and Perry; the block composition returns one. The difference is a shared boundary line, and it is why containment here is settled by counting blocks rather than by asking a spatial query.

**It is older than every village in the county but one.** The county's 1834 tax list assesses Alex. Creps $1.89 on **thirty-six lots in the village of Westminster**, at a valuation of $172. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md), both scans agreeing. A platted village with thirty-six taxable lots in 1834 predates Bluffton by three years, Spencerville by ten and Gomer by sixteen, and is beaten only by [Lima](lima.yml) in 1831. It has never been incorporated in the hundred and ninety years since, which is the difference between this place and the nine that were: they got a corporation and a boundary, and this got a plat and then nothing.

nodes.label: Which congressional district is Allen County in now?

properties.would_close_this: A current county-to-congressional-district relationship file from the Census Bureau, if one is published for the 118th or 119th Congress under a path this corpus has not found; the Ohio Secretary of State's district map, retrieved by hand rather than by an automated client; or the enacted redistricting plan itself, which names its constituent counties.

blocks.text: At the 2020 census, all 3,552 of Allen County's census blocks fell in [Ohio's 4th congressional district](../division/ohio-congressional-district-4-2020.yml). [verified] — [2020 Census Block Assignment Files](../../catalog/census-block-assignment-2020.md).
